author: BBC News
description:
The US central bank has raised interest rates for the first time in three years as inflation rises, driven by higher fuel and energy costs caused by the Iran War. 

President Trump hit out at the decision by the US Federal Reserve, calling on it to “lower rates, and fast!”.

The Fed is seeking to curb rising prices, as the Iran War pushes up global oil and gas prices, hitting American business and consumers. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for business as well as for people with loans, mortgages and credit cards.

Global oil prices have surged since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, driving up the price of car fuel as well as the cost of goods and services generally.  Borrowing costs are rising around the world, with growing warnings of the economic impact on living standards.

Sophie Raworth presents BBC News at Ten reporting by Dharshini David, Sarah Smith and Chris Mason.

He said that he accepted that consultants must bear "collective" responsibility for some of the failings identified in the report.

An oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been temporarily shut down after it was badly damaged in a strike last week.

The pipeline is key to minimising the impact of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on the world’s global oil supply.

Combined with Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, experts are concerned the closure could force oil prices even higher.

Plus, Faisal and Adam look at the growing pushback against AI data centres which could pose a key issue at the US midterms.

Over the last week, the Houthis - an Iran-backed militant group in Yemen - have captured two strategic islands along the Red Sea coast, consolidating its control of a key international shipping route known as the Bab al-Mandab strait. 

Saudi Arabia has relied on access to the strait for exporting its oil to customers in Asia. With the Strait of Hormuz already closed due to the Iran war, the Houthis’ control of this vital waterway threatens to deepen the global oil supply crisis. 

Tristan Redman is joined by the BBC’s Security Correspondent Frank Gardner to unpack who the Houthis are, what they want,  and how they have come to hold so much influence on the world’s economy.

description:
At least 20 people have been killed, including five children, and dozens are missing after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip, according to local rescue teams.

Video footage shows the search for bodies and survivors continuing in the rubble of the multi-storey building in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City, its floors sandwiched together.
 
Locals said 10 families had been living in the apartments despite warnings that they were unsafe.
 
Members of the Hamas-run Civil Defence rescue service said they had initially been working with "empty hands" due to tight Israeli restrictions on equipment allowed into Gaza. However, they have since been able to borrow some heavy machinery.

description:
New figures suggest the state pension will rise by 3.9% to up to £13,000 a year. The increase is based on earning figures as dictated by the triple lock, the policy the government uses to guarantee pension growth.

The rise has reignited debates about the long-term affordability and generational fairness of state pensions which have seen costs balloon in recent years.

Alex and James are joined by economics editor Faisal Islam who’s also been speaking to Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark about calls for greater AI safeguarding.

Plus, the Thirlwall inquiry into how Lucy Letby was able to murder babies at the Countess of Chester hospital has delivered its findings, describing a "complete failure" to protect infants from harm. Michael Buchanan, social affairs correspondent, was at the inquiry and has been following the crisis in UK maternity care.

author: BBC News
description:
US President Donald Trump has said fears about the safety of artificial intelligence (AI) are a "hoax", as he criticised calls to have more guardrails in place for the fast-moving technology.
 
OpenAI boss Sam Altman thinks people should have more faith in his company and others like it to do the right thing when it comes to AI development amid rising public concerns about all the risks.
 
"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.
 
However, Altman noted that people were justified in their fears around AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.
